title: Social System and Social Stratification of Nepalese Societies

toc.title: 3.2 Social and cultural change in Nepal
Model answers: medium (5 marks) and long (10 marks) questions

html:
A social system is not only a list of institutions; it is a set of processes by which people interact and a structure of unequal positions in which they live. This unit has two halves.

The first half covers social processes, socialisation and social and cultural change in Nepal.

The second half studies social stratification in Nepal: caste and ethnicity, gender, religion and ecology, and finally how a diverse country holds together (national integration).

This is the unit in which the course speaks most directly about Nepal. Use the facts with care: laws are cited by name and year; census numbers are approximate and from the 2021 census unless said otherwise.

What this unit gives you
  • Social processes (cooperation, competition, conflict, accommodation, assimilation) and socialisation (agents, theories of Cooley, Mead, Freud).
  • Social and cultural change: types, theories and factors in Nepal, from the 1951 revolution to the 2015 constitution and digital media.
  • Stratification: caste, class, status and power; the Muluki Ain of 1854 and caste, ethnic, gender, religious and ecological stratification in Nepal.
  • National integration: the historical process of nationhood; cultural integration through language, rituals and customs.

3.1 Social system and social processes

A social system is an organised pattern of interrelated statuses, roles, groups and institutions that works as a whole (Talcott Parsons).

Social structure is the framework of positions and the relationships between them; social process is the dynamic side: the repeated forms of interaction by which structure is made, kept and changed.

Sociologists classify social processes as associative (bringing people together) or dissociative (driving them apart).

Process Meaning Example
Cooperation People work together for a common goal Parma labour exchange; an open-source project
Accommodation Adjustment that settles a conflict without removing it; compromise, arbitration, toleration Wage settlement; a code of conduct after a dispute
Assimilation Groups with different cultures merge into one; gradual and often one-way Migrants adopting the language of the host town
Competition Rivalry for scarce goods within rules Students competing for scholarships; firms for customers
Conflict Open struggle to defeat or remove the other party Land disputes; communal violence; strikes

Competition is impersonal and continuous; conflict is personal and intermittent. Georg Simmel showed that conflict may also integrate: a strike can settle rules that later keep peace.

Socialisation

Socialisation is the lifelong process by which a person learns the culture, norms, values and roles of their society and develops a self. Without it, humans do not become social beings (cases of children raised in isolation show the lack of language and social ability).

Agents of socialisation: family (the first and strongest: language, basic values), peer group (equals; norms of dress, slang, risk), school (formal knowledge, discipline, time), religion (moral order, rituals), mass media and the internet (examples and role models), workplace (occupational norms).

Today social media competes with all of them.

Primary socialisation occurs in childhood in the family; secondary socialisation in later life through schools and work; anticipatory socialisation prepares for a future role (BCA students rehearsing professional behaviour); resocialisation replaces earlier patterns (training in military, or migration).

Theorist Idea
Charles Horton Cooley Looking-glass self: we imagine how others see us, imagine their judgement, and respond with pride or shame.
George Herbert Mead The self arises in interaction. Stages: imitation (copying), play stage (taking the role of one significant other), game stage (taking the role of many, the generalised other). The self has an impulsive "I" and a socially aware "Me".
Sigmund Freud Personality has id (instinct), ego (reality) and superego (internalised norms), with socialisation as the control of the id.
Jean Piaget Cognitive development in stages: sensorimotor, preoperational, concrete operational, formal operational.

3.2 Social and cultural change in Nepal

Social change is a change in social structure and relationships, whereas cultural change is a change in beliefs, values, language, art and technology.

They go together but are not identical: a village may adopt mobile phones (material change) while caste norms remain (cultural continuity).

Change can be evolutionary (gradual), revolutionary (rapid and structural), planned (development programmes) or unplanned, and progressive or regressive depending on values.

Theories of change in brief. Evolutionary (Spencer, Comte): societies move from simple to complex. Cyclical (Sorokin, Pareto): societies repeat phases. Functionalist: change restores balance after strain. Conflict (Marx): change comes from class struggle. Modernisation theory: traditional societies move to modern ones through economic growth, education, urbanisation and secular values; dependency theory answers that poor countries are held back by their position in the world economy. Two Indian sociologists' ideas are widely applied to South Asia: M. N. Srinivas's Sanskritisation (lower groups adopting the rituals and customs of higher castes in order to rise) and Westernisation (adoption of Western technology, dress, institutions, ideas).

Factors of social and cultural change in Nepal

Factor How it changes Nepali society Examples
Political events Changes of regime rewrite rights and institutions 1951 end of Rana rule; 1990 Jana Andolan and a multi-party constitution; 2006 People's Movement II; 2008 abolition of monarchy and a republic; 2015 federal, secular constitution
Law and state policy Formal rules change what is acceptable New Muluki Ain 1963 abolished legal caste hierarchy; caste untouchability criminalised by the 2011 Act; Civil Code 2074
Education Literacy, mobility, new aspirations and professions Literacy (age 5 and above) 76.2 per cent in 2021; growth in colleges and BCA programmes
Economy and migration Remittances change household income and land use; urbanisation shifts population Large numbers of workers abroad; growth of Kathmandu, Pokhara, Biratnagar, Butwal
Technology and media New communication, ideas and consumption Radio (community radio from 1997), television, mobile phones, mobile data and social media
Development and infrastructure Roads, electricity and internet link remote areas Rural road networks, hydropower, fibre links
Natural events and disasters Force relocation and new institutions 2015 earthquake and reconstruction
Ideas and movements Rights movements change values Dalit, Janajati, Madhesi, women's movements; inclusion

Resistance to change. Habit, fear of loss, vested interests, rigid norms and lack of resources slow change. The result is cultural lag (Unit 2): new institutions exist on paper while attitudes follow later.

Change through a phone

Within two decades a Nepali village may have moved from letters and landlines to mobile phones, then to mobile money and Facebook video calls. The material change is quick.

The non-material change follows more slowly: who is allowed to own a phone, who controls remittance money, how young people choose spouses, which language is used in messages. Studying change means tracking both layers.

3.3 Social stratification

Social stratification is the structured ranking of individuals and groups into layers (strata) according to wealth, power and prestige, so that some get more of society's rewards.

It is a feature of society, not of individuals; it persists across generations; it is universal but variable; and it is supported by beliefs that justify it.

Systems of stratification. Slavery (people owned as property), caste (closed, ascribed, hereditary, ritual ranking), estate (legally defined orders such as nobles and commoners) and class (open, based on economic position and achievement, with mobility possible).

Nepal has a unique blend: caste hierarchy, ethnic hierarchy, class, gender and region operate together, which is why sociologists use the word intersectionality: a Dalit woman in a remote district faces more than the sum of the separate disadvantages.

Theory Claim
Functionalist (Davis and Moore) Stratification is necessary: society must motivate talented people to fill important and demanding positions, using unequal rewards. Critics say it ignores inheritance of advantage.
Marxist Stratification rests on ownership of the means of production; two main classes (bourgeoisie and proletariat) with conflicting interests.
Weberian Three dimensions: class (economic position), status (prestige and honour) and party (political power). A person can rank high on one and low on another.

Social mobility is movement between strata: vertical (up or down), horizontal (same level, new job), intergenerational (children's position compared with parents') and intragenerational (within one career).

Education, migration and jobs in IT create mobility in Nepal, but caste, region and family wealth still decide who gets the chance.

3.4 Caste and ethnicity based stratification

The traditional hierarchy and the Muluki Ain of 1854

Hindu caste (jat) divides society into ranked, hereditary, endogamous groups with rules of purity, occupation and contact. The traditional varna scheme has four orders (Brahmin, Kshatriya, Vaishya, Shudra) and thousands of jati.

In 1854 Prime Minister Jung Bahadur Rana promulgated the Muluki Ain (Country Code), the first comprehensive legal code of Nepal, which wrote the caste order into state law, with different punishments for the same offence depending on the caste of the offender and victim.

It ranked the population into five broad layers that included the non-Hindu ethnic groups as well:

The text of the code names specific groups under each layer; the figure keeps only the layer names, because the names have changed, and some terms are now offensive.

What matters for the exam is the structure: caste ranking was legal, hereditary and included ethnic groups through the categories of matwali (alcohol-drinkers); the lowest groups, today called Dalits, were treated as untouchable.

Present-day situation

  • Legal change. The new Muluki Ain of 1963 (2020 BS) abolished legal caste discrimination. The Caste-Based Discrimination and Untouchability (Offence and Punishment) Act, 2011 (2068 BS) criminalises untouchability and discrimination; the Constitution of Nepal 2015 (2072 BS) guarantees the right against untouchability (Article 24), the right to equality (Article 18), and inclusion of Dalits in state bodies.
  • Ethnic groups. The 2021 census recorded about 142 caste and ethnic groups and about 124 languages. The government recognises 59 Adivasi Janajati (indigenous nationalities) under the National Foundation for Development of Indigenous Nationalities Act, 2002 (2058 BS). Large groups include Chhetri, Hill Brahmin, Magar, Tharu, Tamang, Newar and the Dalit group.
  • Discrimination persists. Dalits still report denial of temple and water access, restrictions in hotels and houses, and caste violence in some areas; their rates of poverty, landlessness and school dropout are higher than the national average. Janajati groups often face language loss and loss of land and forest rights. Madhesi communities have raised demands for citizenship, representation and identity (movements of 2007 and 2015).
  • Inclusion policy. Civil service open competition seats are reserved in a quota: women 33 per cent, Adivasi Janajati 27, Madhesi 22, Dalit 9, persons with disability 5, backward regions 4. The Constitution (Article 42) provides the right to social justice and inclusion; the House of Representatives has mixed first-past-the-post and proportional inclusive seats.
Caste, class and technology

Caste is not a code in a database, yet systems encode it silently: a surname field can reveal caste; face recognition and recruitment tools trained on unequal data can repeat historic exclusions; information is not equally available in Nepali, Maithili or Tharu.

Digital inclusion work (Units 6 and 7) is a social-justice task as well as a technical one.

3.5 Gender based stratification

Sex is biological; gender is the social meaning attached to being male or female: roles, expectations and unequal access to resources. Patriarchy is a social system in which men hold primary power.

In Nepal patriarchal norms have shaped property, marriage, education, mobility and work.

Area Situation and change
Law The Constitution (2015) guarantees equality, the rights of women (Article 38), and at least 33 per cent women in the federal parliament. The Country Code's reforms from 2002 and the Civil Code 2074 give daughters equal inheritance rights; marriage age is 20 for both. Domestic Violence (Offence and Punishment) Act 2066, the criminalisation of chhaupadi (menstrual seclusion) in the Criminal Code 2074 (in force 2018).
Education Girls' enrolment has risen, nearly equal in basic education; gaps persist in science and technology streams and in higher education.
Work Women do much unpaid care and farm labour; formal ownership of land and houses by women is low (rises with tax incentives on registration). Women are a small minority in IT jobs.
Politics Local-level elections of 2017 brought a large number of women, including 40 per cent of ward-level reserved seats, to local government.
Violence Domestic violence, trafficking, dowry harassment, witchcraft accusations and online abuse remain concerns.
Third gender The Supreme Court (2007, Sunil Babu Pant case) recognised a third gender; the 2015 constitution recognises sexual and gender minorities' rights and citizenship certificates with "other".
Gender and digital

A women's group in a hill municipality uses a mobile app to manage savings. The app works well, but the phone belongs to the household head and charging, data and the PIN are controlled by him.

The social conditions of access decide whether the technology empowers or not. Sociologists call this the gender digital divide (Unit 6).

3.6 Religion-based and ecology-based stratification

Religion-based stratification

Nepal is a secular state under Article 4 of the 2015 constitution, and the Census 2021 shows a plural religious landscape.

The constitution defines secularity as protection of religion and culture inherited from ancient times, so the state is neither anti-religious nor tied to one faith.

Religion (Census 2021) Share of population Note
Hinduism 81.19 per cent Majority religion; the state was officially Hindu until 2006-2008
Buddhism 8.21 per cent Janajati groups of the hills and mountains, and Lumbini as the birthplace of the Buddha
Islam 5.09 per cent Mostly in the Terai, with smaller hill communities
Kirat 3.17 per cent Indigenous faith of Rai, Limbu and others
Christianity 1.76 per cent Fastest growing in the last three censuses
Others under 1 per cent Prakriti (nature worship), Bon, Jain, Bahai and Sikh

Where does stratification come from? Religion creates inequality when one faith's calendar, symbols and law are treated as the national default. Historically the Hindu state gave the ruling castes a legal advantage (Section 3.4). Today the issues are more subtle:

  • Public holidays and the calendar. Most national holidays follow the Hindu calendar; Eid, Christmas, Buddha Jayanti, Lhosar and Udhauli/Ubhauli are recognised in different degrees.
  • Conversion. Article 26 of the constitution protects religious freedom but forbids converting another person; the Muluki Criminal Code 2074 punishes it. Critics say the provision restricts missionary work and can be misused against minorities; supporters say it protects social harmony.
  • Cow slaughter. The criminal code still treats cow slaughter as an offence, a rule rooted in Hindu belief that Muslims and some Janajati communities find hard to accept.
  • Cemetery and cremation land. Burial grounds for Muslims, Christians and Kirat communities have often been hard to secure, a daily reminder that a minority needs land, not only rights on paper.
  • Language of ritual and schooling. Sanskrit and Hindu texts occupy a large space in schooling, while madrasa and gumba education has found it hard to gain recognition.

Interfaith life in practice. A tourist in Kathmandu sees Hindu temples and Buddhist stupas sharing the same courtyard (Swayambhu, Boudhanath, Pashupati), a harmony many Nepalis cite as national strength.

Social scientists therefore speak of syncretism: the mixing of practices from different traditions, particularly among Newar Buddhists and Hindus.

Ecology-based stratification

Nepal is divided into three ecological belts that run east-west: Mountain (Himal), Hill (Pahad) and Terai. Roughly 6 in 100 people live in the mountains, 40 in the hills and 54 in the Terai (Census 2021).

Each belt has its own climate, farming system and communities.

Ecological stratification means that where a person lives decides access to roads, schools, health care, electricity, markets and the internet, in addition to caste, class and gender.

Belt Typical features Typical disadvantage
Mountain Highest altitude, sparse population, herding, trekking tourism, cold winters Long distances to hospital and school; hard and costly to build roads and towers; seasonal isolation
Hill Terraced farming, many towns and valleys, strong out-migration Dispersed settlements; landslides; youth leave and old people stay
Terai Plains, most fertile and most populated, border with India, strong market links Floods; caste and gender inequality; high landlessness among Dalit and Madhesi groups; language and citizenship issues

Technology and the ecological divide. Mobile-tower coverage and fibre follow population and roads. A mountain district can have the strongest need for telemedicine and online classes and the weakest signal.

Planning therefore compares per-capita access between belts and between provinces (Karnali and Sudurpaschim usually score lowest on development indicators; Bagmati and Gandaki highest).

Reading a ranking correctly

Two districts have 80 per cent mobile-phone coverage. In the first, 20 per cent of households have electricity for fewer than four hours a day; in the second, none. Coverage alone hides the quality of access.

A responsible analyst reports coverage, reliability, price and skill together, which is why the Unit 6 digital-divide measures use several indicators and not one.

3.7 National integration

National integration is the process of bringing the culturally, linguistically, religiously and regionally different groups of a country into a shared sense of belonging without erasing their differences.

A nation is "imagined" (Benedict Anderson): people who will never meet feel they belong together because of shared symbols, media and institutions.

Historical process of nationhood

Phase Event Effect on integration
Before 1768 Many small principalities (the Baise and Chaubise rajya) in the hills; Malla kingdoms in the Kathmandu valley Each region had its own rulers, languages and customs
1768-1816 Unification led by Prithvi Narayan Shah, who conquered Kathmandu in 1768; expansion ended with the Sugauli Treaty of 1816 Created a single state with approximately today's borders; his Dibya Upadesh described Nepal as a garden of four varnas and thirty-six jats
1846-1951 Rana rule; the Muluki Ain of 1854 fixed a caste hierarchy Integrated the territory but ranked the people
1951-1960 End of Rana rule; early democratic experiment Opened the state to wider participation
1960-1990 Panchayat system; the slogan one language, one dress, one nation; Nepali promoted in schools and media Built a common language and symbols but suppressed minority languages and identities; many groups felt excluded
1990 and after Constitution of 1990 recognised a multi-ethnic and multilingual nation; Jana Andolan II (2006), republic (2008) Moved from assimilation to recognition of diversity
2015 Constitution of Nepal: federal, secular, inclusive; all mother tongues are languages of the nation Integration is now defined as unity in diversity

Cultural integration: language, rituals and customs

  • Language. The 2021 census recorded 124 mother tongues. Nepali is the language of government, the lingua franca of the country and the common medium between groups. The constitution allows provinces to choose additional official languages; this is called the language policy of recognition. Technology matters here: Unicode, Nepali keyboards, voice typing and machine translation decide whether minority languages enter the digital world (Unit 6, Section 6.3).
  • Rituals and festivals. Dashain, Tihar, Holi, Chhath, Eid, Buddha Jayanti, Lhosar, Christmas, Maghe Sankranti and others are shared across regions; the way each community adds its own colour (Newar Indra Jatra, Tharu Maghi, Kirat Udhauli) is cultural exchange.
  • Customs and dress. The daura-suruwal and dhaka topi became symbols of the nation in the Panchayat era, while communities keep their own dress for festivals. The same national symbol can be both unifying and exclusionary if it is imposed.
  • Shared institutions. The national flag (the only non-rectangular national flag in the world), anthem, army, airline, Nepali cinema, cricket and football all give people a shared story.

Barriers to integration. Regional inequality, caste discrimination, language dominance, political polarisation, a weak sense of ownership of the state among excluded groups, and fake news and hate speech spread through social media that harden identity lines.

How technology helps. Community FM radio in many languages, TikTok, YouTube and Facebook groups let a Tharu singer, a Tamang filmmaker and a Maithili poet reach the whole country, and let the diaspora stay in touch.

This is integration by choice, in contrast to the integration by imposition of the Panchayat era.

Chapter summary

  • A social system is an organised pattern of statuses, roles, groups and institutions. The social processes are cooperation, competition, conflict, accommodation and assimilation; socialisation turns a newborn into a member of society (Cooley, Mead, Freud, Piaget).
  • Social change alters structure and relationships; cultural change alters beliefs, language and technology. In Nepal the main factors are politics, law, education, migration, technology and media, infrastructure, disasters and rights movements.
  • Stratification is a ranking of people into layers with unequal rewards. Nepal's formal caste hierarchy (Muluki Ain 1854) was abolished by the Muluki Ain 1963; discrimination persists and is criminalised.
  • Caste, ethnicity, gender, religion and ecology each create unequal access, and they overlap.
  • National integration moved from imposed assimilation (one language, one dress, one nation) to unity in diversity under the 2015 constitution.

Practice

  1. Define social system. Name its elements.
  2. List the five social processes with one example each.
  3. What is socialisation? Name four agents of socialisation.
  4. State Cooley's looking-glass self and Mead's stages of the self.
  5. Differentiate social change from cultural change.
  6. Write down five factors of social and cultural change in Nepal.
  7. Define social stratification. How does caste differ from class?
  8. What was the Muluki Ain of 1854 and what replaced it?
  9. Describe two problems that Dalit communities face and one legal protection against them.
  10. How do ecological belts create stratification in Nepal?
  11. What does the constitution say about secularism, and what are the issues for religious minorities?
  12. Define national integration and explain how the policy changed after 1990.
Answers and worked solutions

1. A social system is an organised pattern of interrelated statuses, roles, groups and institutions that functions as a whole. Elements: statuses and roles, norms and values, groups, institutions, social control.

2. Cooperation (parma, open-source teamwork); competition (students for a scholarship); conflict (land disputes, strikes); accommodation (a wage settlement); assimilation (a migrant adopting the host language).

3. Socialisation is the lifelong process of learning the culture, norms and roles of society. Agents: family, peer group, school, mass media and the internet, religion, workplace.

4. Cooley: we imagine how others see us, imagine their judgement, and feel pride or shame. Mead: imitation, play stage, game stage (generalised other); the self has an I and a Me.

5. Social change is a change in social structure and relationships; cultural change is a change in beliefs, values, language, art and technology. Example: a village can adopt phones (cultural-material) while caste rules continue (no social change).

6. Political events, law, education, migration and remittances, technology and media, infrastructure, disasters, social movements (any five).

7. Stratification ranks people into layers with unequal wealth, power and prestige. Caste is ascribed by birth and closed; class is based on economic position and open to movement.

8. The Muluki Ain 1854 was the first national legal code, which fixed a caste hierarchy and applied different punishments by caste. The New Muluki Ain 1963 treated all citizens equally in law; the Caste-based Discrimination and Untouchability Act 2011 made discrimination a crime.

9. Problems: exclusion from temples, water sources and jobs; landlessness and poverty. Protection: Article 24 of the constitution and the 2011 Act (see Section 3.4).

10. Mountain, hill and Terai differ in road, health, school and network access, so where one lives affects opportunity as strongly as caste or income.

11. Article 4 declares Nepal secular, meaning protection of inherited religion and culture, with Article 26 on freedom and the ban on conversion. Issues: public holidays, conversion offences, burial land.

12. National integration is the process of creating a common sense of belonging while respecting differences. Before 1990 the policy was assimilation; the 1990 and 2015 constitutions recognised diversity and all mother tongues as national languages.

Model answers: medium (5 marks) and long (10 marks) questions

Q1 (5 marks). What is socialisation? Explain the agents of socialisation.

Meaning. Socialisation is the process by which an individual learns the language, values, norms and roles of society and becomes a social being. It continues from birth to death.

Agents. The family gives language and first values. The peer group teaches equality, belonging and fashion. The school teaches knowledge, discipline and citizenship.

The mass media and social media transmit information and shape taste and opinion; they are now among the strongest agents for the young. Religion and the workplace teach moral codes and professional behaviour.

Q2 (10 marks). Define social stratification. Explain caste and ethnicity-based stratification in Nepal.

Definition. Social stratification is the hierarchical arrangement of individuals and groups in society according to wealth, power and prestige, a structure that persists across generations.

Caste system. In Nepal the Hindu caste system divided people into four varnas and numerous jats; the Muluki Ain of 1854 fixed the hierarchy into law (the "wearers of the holy cord" at the top, and "water-unacceptable and untouchable" castes at the bottom).

The 1963 code abolished legal inequality and the 2011 Act criminalised caste-based discrimination, but Dalits, who are about 13 per cent of the population, still face lower income, land, literacy and political representation.

Ethnicity. Janajati communities (Tharu, Tamang, Newar, Magar, Rai, Limbu and others) were classed as "enslavable" or "non-enslavable alcohol-drinking" groups in the 1854 code, lost land and language under assimilation and now press for recognition, autonomy and proportional participation (the Madhesi and Janajati movements of 2006-2015).

Conclusion. Caste is closed and ascribed, class open and achieved; in Nepal they overlap. Inclusive provisions of the 2015 constitution, reservation in civil service and education, and awareness campaigns are narrowing the gap, but implementation remains the test.

Q3 (5 marks). Explain national integration and the role of language and rituals.

National integration is a process of unifying a diverse population into one nation while retaining differences.

In Nepal, history moved from the unification of 1768 and the one-language policy of the Panchayat to the 2015 constitution that recognises all mother tongues as languages of the nation.

Language provides a common medium (Nepali) and identity (mother tongues); rituals and festivals such as Dashain, Tihar, Eid, Lhosar and Buddha Jayanti create shared occasions while keeping local colour.

Integration is strong when each group feels the nation is its own.
